strengths: Addresses important problem of multi-objective LLM alignment across diverse domain types (verifiable, non-verifiable, interactive)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct domains with proper methodology (3 runs, standard deviations, multiple baselines)
Practical contributions enabling dynamic inference-time objective weighting without retraining
Elegant technical solution for continuing hidden state in PRM decoding, with valid computational analysis
Thorough reproducibility support with detailed appendices, system prompts, and implementation details
Clear findings on how reward verifiability guides method selection (training vs. test-time optimization)
Well-motivated gradient analysis showing isolated head optimization with shared backbone accumulation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—PRM hindsight relabeling is straightforward RL adaptation, MAH-DPO is natural but not novel combination of DPO with per-head losses

Problematic evaluation for non-verifiable domains: LLM-as-Judge achieves only 75.8% accuracy; Bradley-Terry models lack validation against actual user preferences; Socratic Mind uses circular student simulation on same data distribution
Unified PRM framework contradicted by results—unified model consistently underperforms specialized PRMs across all objectives/domains (Figure 4), undermining unification premise
Modest empirical improvements with insufficient statistical rigor: many gains 1-5% and fall within error margins; no significance testing reported
Incomplete technical specification: boundary detection criteria Q in Algorithm 1 never formally defined; case selection (A/B/C) for non-verifiable PRMs appears post-hoc rather than principled
Limited scope: only 3 domains, no recent multi-objective RL comparisons beyond MODPO, small models (7-8B), no ablations on action head counts or head specialization analysis
Contradictions between claims and results: Figure 3 shows performance degradation when objectives not emphasized, contradicting smooth control claim; Finding 6 shows correlation not causation
Missing failure analysis: no discussion of when method fails, sensitivity to PRM quality, or scaling behavior

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: simultaneous multi-objective alignment of LLMs across verifiable and non-verifiable domains
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (math, human values, tutoring) with extensive ablations, robustness analyses, and human validation
Well-engineered framework with practical contributions: standardized PRM training pipeline, Multi-Action-Head DPO design, and efficient continuing hidden-state decoding (4.9× speedup)
Key actionable insight (Finding 7): verifiable rewards benefit more from test-time search while subjective rewards benefit from training-time modeling
Solid technical execution with thorough appendices providing implementation details, hyperparameters, and full results with standard deviations
Demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple objectives simultaneously with limited interference, without requiring retraining
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Multi-Action-Head is straightforward (separate linear projections); PRM training follows standard practices; components are from prior work (Rafailov et al. 2023, Andrychowicz et al. 2018). Innovation is primarily in engineering and integration rather than novel methods
Modest empirical improvements: Math accuracy 0.7107→0.7247 (2%), Human Values 0.5800→0.6389 (10% via ensemble); unclear if gains justify added complexity

Evaluation reliability concerns: Heavy reliance on LLM-as-Judge for subjective dimensions with moderate agreement (κ=0.45 in human validation, Table 22); annotator disagreement ranges 39%-80%; experiments limited to 7B-8B models, scalability unclear

Overstated claims: 'Unified PRM' is strictly dominated by specialized PRMs on all dimensions (Figure 4)—marketed as success but clearly a failure; 'standardized pipeline' is actually tailored to three specific domains with significant methodological differences

Insufficient justification of design choices: head initialization strategy, equal objective weights during training, γ=0.9 discount factor, β=0.1 DPO parameter all lack ablation studies or justification; these could significantly impact results
Limited baseline comparisons: Only MODPO and DPO Soup as main baselines; missing comparisons to other recent multi-objective methods; no simple multi-task learning baselines

Scaling concerns: Only tested up to 5 objectives; no analysis of gradient variance with more heads; unclear when shared backbone capacity becomes limiting; catastrophic failure of Single Head DPO (Table 2) not deeply analyzed
PRM quality dependency: Method heavily depends on PRM quality but doesn't provide deep guidance on ensuring good PRM training, especially for non-verifiable domains with inherently noisy labels
Missing practical guidance: How to choose objective weights at deployment time? What happens with fundamentally misaligned objectives? No analysis of failure modes or performance degradation cases

strengths: Well-motivated problem with systematic solution: Clear three-way categorization of domains (verifiable/non-verifiable/unclear) with tailored PRM training approaches
Technically sound multi-action-head architecture: Gradient isolation via head routing prevents objective conflicts that plague scalarization methods, with clear mathematical analysis (Eq. 7)
Continuing hidden state approach: Elegant solution providing 4× speedup for decoding while maintaining generation continuity, avoiding discontinuities from prompt re-encoding

Comprehensive experimental validation: Three diverse domains (math, values, tutoring) with strong baselines (MODPO, DPO Soup), extensive ablations (segmentation robustness, noise sensitivity, cross-model validation)
Actionable insights: Finding 7 provides valuable guidance that verifiable rewards benefit from test-time search while subjective rewards benefit from training-time shaping
Excellent reproducibility: Complete implementation details, hyperparameters, system prompts in appendices; IRB approval and privacy protections documented
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective figures, organized appendices, and good motivation for multi-objective alignment's real-world importance
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: Multi-action heads are straightforward architectural extensions; PRM training builds directly on Math-Shepherd; cache continuation is engineering optimization not algorithmic innovation

PRM quality dependency and robustness gaps: Engagement drops 16% under 50% label noise (71.87% → 59.80%); unified PRM never outperforms specialized PRMs; no guidance for constructing PRMs in novel domains

Severely limited human evaluation: Only 100 math samples with moderate agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.45); critically, NO human evaluation for Human Values or Socratic Mind—these entirely rely on automated LLM-as-Judge, creating circularity risk
Modest empirical improvements in key domains: Human Values improvements ~1-2% over MODPO; Socratic Mind gains smaller than Math; some gains within noise margins given reported standard deviations

Scalability uncertainties and design choices lacking justification: Only tested to 5 objectives; discount factors (γ ∈ {0.9, 0.95}) and perturbation scales (0.001-0.005) appear arbitrary without ablation studies; limited guidance on objective selection or failure modes

Incomplete analysis of objective interactions: No systematic framework predicting when objectives complement vs. conflict; qualitative examples provided but lack principled approach; no discussion of catastrophic forgetting when adding objectives

Evaluation metric concerns: Heavy reliance on LLM-as-Judge (Qwen-based) for non-verifiable objectives; same model family used for training and evaluation (except F.1); potential model bias alignment with training objectives
